title: New Texas Social Studies Standards Are Content-Specific but Divisive
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler — author of The Knowledge Gap and one of the most credible voices on knowledge-based curriculum — examines Texas's newly approved social studies standards, which arrive at the politically charged intersection of content-rich curriculum advocacy and culture-war curriculum politics. The standards are notable for being genuinely content-specific in ways that most state standards are not: they name specific events, people, documents, and places that students are expected to know, aligning with the knowledge-building argument that vague skill-based standards produce shallow, inequitable learning. Wexler acknowledges this as a genuine improvement over the abstract, skill-focused standards that currently dominate most states. However, the Texas standards also embed specific patriotic and religious framings that reflect Texas's political majority rather than scholarly consensus — creating a situation where the structural advance (content-specificity) is bundled with political content choices that make the standards difficult to defend or replicate in other states. The article is Wexler's attempt to hold both truths simultaneously: the standards represent real progress on content-richness, and their politicization represents a genuine problem both for Texas students and for the broader movement to establish content-based curriculum as a non-partisan educational imperative.
points: Content-specificity is the genuine advance in the Texas standards: unlike most state standards, which name vague skills that can be applied to any content, Texas's standards name specific events, people, documents, and places — which is precisely what the knowledge-building research says is necessary for equitable and durable learning.

The bundling of content-specificity with partisan political framing is the standards' core problem: it makes it nearly impossible to advocate for what's genuinely good about them without appearing to endorse their political content choices, undermining the bipartisan coalition that content-rich curriculum needs to scale nationally.

Wexler's most important implication is about coalition-building: every time content-rich standards get adopted through a partisan process and with partisan content, it makes it harder to argue that knowledge-based curriculum is a universal educational good rather than a culture-war vehicle.

The Texas experience is a case study in how good pedagogical principles can get captured by political processes: the structural insight (students need to know specific things, not just practice skills) was sound, but the specific content choices reflect one political perspective rather than scholarly consensus.

For educators in other states, the lesson is that content-specificity is separable from partisan content selection: it is possible to build knowledge-rich, content-specific standards without embedding them in a particular cultural or religious narrative — and doing so is essential for the knowledge-building movement to survive political capture.
quotes: Just in time for the nation’s 250th birthday, the Texas State Board of Education has approved new social studies standards [ ]that are designed to foster patriotism—and are already exacerbating partisan division. As with its recent approval of a required reading list [ ] for K-12 public schools, the Texas SBOE’s action [ ] on K-8 social studies standards has been a lightning rod for criticism, particularly from the left.

It lists four “conceptual topics,” like “Change, Continuity and Context.” “Notably missing,” the Fordham report observes drily, “is any reference to historical content.” Meanwhile, the performance of American students on national assessments in U.S. history and civics have been abysmal, with only 13 [ ] and 22 percent [ ] of eighth graders scoring proficient in those subjects, respectively.

And the new standards are clearly more coherent than the ones they’re replacing The standards may not give as much attention to non-Western history and historically disadvantaged or marginalized groups as some would like, and they do focus a lot on Christianity. But they cover more non-Western and non-Christian topics than critics acknowledge.

In any event, the pressure to make these connections results in some spiraling because aspects of American and Texas history and government are constantly popping up, sometimes in unexpected places. during whatever era the standards are covering can also distort priorities.

In any event, for all the impassioned debate over the standards, much will depend on how—and to what extent—they’re actually taught. Because few states require testing in social studies, standards for that subject often just sit on a shelf, or its digital equivalent, at least until high school.

If they haven’t—and it’s likely many will not, unless Texas starts testing social studies earlier—it could be a disaster. As with the new Texas required reading list [ ], much of the intent behind the new social studies standards was admirable: to provide educators with the specifics that will ensure the state’s 5.5 million students get a content-rich, rigorous education.
